items.title: RSV vaccines slash infections: data show jabs’ staggering success against dangerous virus
items.author: Liam Drew
items.summary: New data from Denmark and global health estimates demonstrate that RSV vaccines and monoclonal antibody treatments are significantly reducing infant hospitalizations. Experts describe the rapid development of these preventative measures as an 'embarrassment of riches' for public health.

brief.what: Recent clinical data, including a study from Denmark, show that nationwide RSV vaccination programs for pregnant people and monoclonal antibody injections for high-risk infants have led to a sharp decline in hospital admissions. Globally, the WHO reports that RSV causes 3.6 million hospitalizations and 100,000 deaths in children under five annually, with the vast majority occurring in low- and middle-income countries.
brief.who: Epidemiologist Caroline Klint Johannesen and her research team analyzed Danish health records, while the World Health Organization and CDC provided global and US-specific mortality estimates.
brief.context: RSV is a respiratory pathogen that typically causes mild symptoms but poses severe risks to infants and older adults. Until recently, there were no preventative mechanisms available, but regulators have now approved multiple vaccines and monoclonal antibodies.
brief.why: The development of these tools was driven by the urgent need to prevent severe disease in vulnerable populations, with experts noting a shift from having no preventative options to an 'embarrassment of riches' in available treatments.
brief.next: Efforts must now focus on expanding access to these preventative measures in lower-income countries, where the disease burden is highest.
